# Clinical ethics consultation services: public-facing information on NCI-designated cancer center websites

**Authors:** Erica Koranteng; Colin Cernik; Erin Gallagher; Andrew Hantel; Jonathan Marron; Gregory Abel

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Population Sciences, Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, United States | 2 Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | 3Division of Population Sciences, Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, United States | 4Division of Population Sciences, Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, United States | 5Division of Population Sciences, Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, United States | 6 Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | 7 Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | 8 Boston’s Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA, United States | 9Division of Population Sciences, Medical Oncology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, United States | 10 Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | 11Division of Hematologic Malignancies, Medical Oncology, Dana Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, United States

## Abstract

Clinical ethics consultation services (CECS) can be particularly complex in oncology, and widespread misconceptions exist about their nature. As a result, visibility and accessibility of information regarding CECS is critical. We investigated the availability and content of information regarding CECS on websites of NCI-designated comprehensive cancer centers and cancer centers (CCs). Each website was reviewed for information on CECS and reviewed for benchmarks partially derived from the American Society of Bioethics and Humanities recommendations for CECS. Our analysis revealed that of 70 NCI-designated center websites, 38 had information on CECS, and 17 were found directly on these sites. When CECS information was available, most websites provided a mission statement (71%) and an explanation of what constitutes an ethics consult (74%). Few provided a description of the consult process (45%) or service membership (39%). Our findings reveal a significant gap in CECS visibility on the websites of NCI-designated CCs.

Keywords: clinical ethics consultation services, comprehensive cancer center, CCCs, patient care, public information

## Abstract

This article describes information found on NCI-designated cancer center public-facing websites regarding clinical ethics consultation services, focusing on potential deficiencies and ways to improve.

This study describes the information found on NCI-designated cancer center (CC) public-facing websites regarding clinical ethics consultation services (CECS). Our findings highlight the need for CC websites to include comprehensive information regarding CECS and provide information about the domains frequently covered on CECS webpages. While our study is not proscriptive, the identified deficiencies found can be considered in the creation of informative CC CECS webpages and inform further research to develop a formal checklist for CECS webpages.

## Introduction

The Joint Commission on the Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations requires hospitals to have a mechanism for addressing ethical issues that arise during patient care, such as through clinical ethics consultation services (CECS).1 In cancer care, these consultations can be particularly complex due to disease-related stigma and a rapidly evolving treatment landscape.2,3 CECS that attend to these specialized needs can be beneficial but require that their presence and purpose be known. As a result, CECS visibility and accessibility by potential users—including clinicians, patients, and families—is critical.4,5

The National Cancer Institute (NCI) has designated 54 comprehensive cancer centers (CCCs) and 11 cancer centers (CCs). Both types of institutions (which we will refer to collectively as NCI-designated centers) “develop and translate scientific knowledge from promising laboratory discoveries into new treatments…and serve their local communities with programs and services tailored to their unique needs and populations.”6 In the modern oncology treatment era, the internet is the predominant source of health information,7,8 with websites often the first point of contact between hospitals and the public. Accordingly, the CECS information on NCI-designated center websites should be a gold standard for all CCs to emulate.

For CECS, the American Society of Bioethics and Humanities (ASBH) sets core competencies and standards9 which have been widely adopted.10 These include a “facilitation” approach, which is a systematic process of conducting consultations and open access to all stakeholders with information on how to access the service. In addition, others have argued that when creating an ethics consultation service, a mission statement should be developed and public-facing information provided, including the membership and leadership of the service.11 In the above context, we aimed to evaluate CECS information on NCI-designated center websites.

## Methods

In August 2023, names and web domains for each NCI-designated center were obtained from the NCI website (https://www.cancer.gov/research/infrastructure/cancer-centers). Each linked website was reviewed for information on its CECS, first assessing if there was an associated ethics department or service on the landing page, and if not available, using each website’s search function with the following terms: “ethics consultation service,” “ethics committee,” “ethics,” or “ethic.” Some webpages found with this method were subdomains of parent/affiliated organizations—for example, our search of the University of Virginia CCC webpage led to a link to the CECS webpage for the University of Virginia School of Medicine. In addition, some NCI Centers did not have any dedicated CECS information found by this method; in those cases, if there was a link on the CCC or CC landing page to a parent/affiliated organization’s website, we searched there as well using the same search terms. The goal was to simulate the experience of a lay user starting on the NCI-designated center website. For consortia, such as the Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center, each hospital within the consortium was evaluated independently.

NCI-designated centers that had CECS webpages were subsequently analyzed according to metrics developed from published ethics consultation service guidelines10,11 as well as the ethics consultation experiences of the authors. These included whether sites presented information about the CECS mission statement, what an ethics consult is, the consult process, contact information, confidentiality, and who can request a consult. We also examined specific website language (including terms used by ASBH such as “facilitation”9) and reading level (Table 1). Websites were independently searched and analyzed by 2 researchers (E.K., E.G.) and conflicts among the 2 were resolved by a third (G.A.). Interobserver agreement before adjudication was assessed with Cohen’s Kappa.

All categorical fields were reported via descriptive statistics with frequencies and percentages, and a 95% CI. We also performed stratified analyses by the presence of a CECS mission statement as well as the presence of CECS information specifically on a cancer website (vs an affiliated/parent site) using Fisher’s exact testing.

## Results

In total, there were 70 NCI-designated centers’ websites reviewed. Of these, 53 were CCCs, 7 were websites of hospitals within CCC consortia, and 10 were CCs. Of the 70 websites searched, 38 (54%) mentioned a CECS on a dedicated webpage, a section on a webpage, or a brief sentence (Supplementary Material). Seventeen of the 38 webpages were specifically on an NCI-designated center website, and 21 were on affiliated/parent website.

For all metrics, pre-adjudication interobserver agreement was moderately strong (range for Cohen’s Kappa between 0.73 and 0.90). CECS webpages most often provided an explanation of what constitutes an ethics consult (74%) and included a mission statement (71%; Table 1). Forty-five percent provided a description of the ethics consult process while 50% used descriptive wording such as “active listening” or “facilitation.” Members of the CECS were listed in 58%, with 39% explicitly stating who led the service. Additionally, 74% stated who could request an ethics consult (eg, patient, family, and clinicians). Website readability was generally poor, with an average Flesch Kincaid Grade Level Score of 13.7.

Compared to websites without mission statements (N = 11), those with mission statements (N = 27) were more likely to present a description of ethics consultation (P = .02), use terms preferred by the ASBH (P = .03) and list members of the CECS team (P = .03). In addition, when CECS details were provided on a dedicated NCI-designated center website (N = 17) rather than a parent/affiliated site (N = 21), they were more likely to describe the ethics consult process (P < .05), provide contact information (P = .005) and use ASBH terms (P < .05; Table 2).

## Discussion

In this cross-sectional analysis of NCI-designated center websites, about half (46%) had no information on CECS on their websites. This is a missed opportunity to inform the public about the presence of ethics consultation services, consistent with the goal of NCI-designated centers to “serve their local communities with programs and services tailored to their unique needs and populations.”6 While ethics consult requests are predominantly made by clinicians (who could seek this information elsewhere),5 public-facing information should also be available for patients with cancer and their families to help them understand what a consult is and potentially access these services.

A mission statement for a CECS communicates the focus of the service, setting the basic parameters of what types of consultation are offered, and serves as a measure of accountability.4,11 We found that 70% of CECS webpages included a mission statement, and when this was present the webpage was more likely to also include detailed information about what an ethics consult is and list the members of the CECS.

The ASBH standards for CECS include open access to all parties involved in patient care as well as a systematic process for conducting consults.10 A clear definition and goal of an ethics consultation as well as a facilitation approach which emphasizes open communication and resolution are also delineated.10 Most NCI-designated centers webpages with CECS information described what an ethics consult is; however, few provided a description of the consult process or used wording that emphasized the facilitation approach favored by the ASBH. On the surface, this seems like a marked deficit, but it is important to attend to the fact that such descriptions can be difficult as there is no “one-size fits all” CECS approach. For example, a website may not mention the CECS process because the method may change according to the issue being addressed (such as when a different method is used for a conflict resolution situation versus a situation about uncertainty about values). It still may be informative to provide a summary of the methods often favored by the service as well as a disclaimer that the methodology is subject to change.

In this study, we operationalized access to the consult service as provision of contact information; however, there could be other methods of establishing contact such as a weblink to a form that is subsequently sent to the service. A large proportion of webpages did provide some form of contact information. Reading grade levels for CECS webpages were well above the fifth to sixth grade level recommended for patient-facing health related information.12 Considering widespread misconceptions surrounding ethics consultations, demystifying the process in plain language seems essential.

Confidentiality and privacy surrounding ethics consultation is also complex, especially in the era of open notes.13 While there is widespread consensus regarding confidentiality of medical data, ambiguity arises when considering the confidentiality of other CECS characteristics such as who requests a consult and the details of the ethical analysis itself.14,15 We found that only 26% of CECS webpages explicitly mentioned confidentiality in relation to ethics consultations.

Given the potential for subspecialty services such as oncology to develop relevant experience, the case has been made for the creation of subspecialty-specific CECS.16 In addition, the importance of specific oncology training for clinical ethicists has been underscored.2,3 We found that CECS information on CC websites (as compared to affiliated institution sites) was more likely to describe the ethics consultation process and use descriptive (and what might be considered helpful) language about the process, such as facilitation and communication. Indeed, all health care institutions should have adequate information about their CECS on their website, and future studies should assess other specialties who may have different bioethical needs.

Our study has limitations. First, the absence of information on NCI-designated center websites does not imply the absence of a CECS, although having a CECS but failing to provide public-facing information about it seems to be at odds with the spirit of NCI CC and CCC designation and perhaps even with ethics consultation itself. Second, it is unclear which category of individuals—patients, families, or clinicians—are more likely to refer to a hospital webpage as a source of information for CECS, and it might be argued that higher reading levels are appropriate for a clinician audience. Finally, the ASBH guidelines that informed several of our reviewing metrics cater to quality ethics consultation services, and not specifically to how information is shared on public websites.

Our aim was to describe what currently exists on NCI-designated CC websites about CECS. Given our results and ASBH guidance, it seems reasonable that cancer related CECS webpages include information across the following domains: mission statement, ethics consultation description as well as some commonly favored methods, contact information, and membership of the service. In the future, a formal checklist might be developed taking into consideration the various ways these can be operationalized; such a checklist would require further qualitative research for its development and validation.

## Conclusion

Many NCI-designated centers lack information about CECS on their websites and when it is available, it is often incomplete and/or presented at high reading levels. Publicly accessible websites are one way of increasing the visibility of CECS. For CCs, they are an excellent opportunity to provide education on some of the commonly encountered ethical issues in oncology and communicate the CECS mission and goals.
